¶
'''telfordize''' (tel′ford-īz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''telfordized'', ppr. ''telfordizing''. In ''road-making'', to construct according to the method of road-making invented by Thomas Telford. See ''Telford pavement''.

¶
'''Telford pavement.''' A roadway devised by the Scotch engineer Thomas Telford (1757–1834).
{{smaller block|The bottoming of the road consists of any durable stone, from 4 to 7 inches in dimensions, hand-laid upon the road-foundation. Between such stones smaller pieces are packed to complete a compact layer 7 inches deep in the middle of the road, and graduated to 4 inches in depth at the sides, to produce a uniform convexity. Upon this is spread, and rolled down, gravel composed of flints, the pieces being as nearly cubical in form as can be obtained, and none weighing more than six ounces. The rolling is continued till the surface is crushed and compacted to smoothness. The name is often contracted to ''telford''.}}

¶
'''telic''' (tel′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. τελικός, final, < τέλος, end, completion.] Noting a final end or purpose. See ''ecbatic''.

¶
'''teliconograph''' (tel-ī-kon′ō-grȧf), ''n.'' [< Gr. τῆλε, afar, + εἰκών, an image, + γράφειν, write. Cf. ''iconograph''.] Same as ''teleiconograph''.

¶
'''Telifera''' (tē-lif′e-rä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < L. ''tela'', web, + ''ferre'' = E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''Epithelaria''.

'''telling''' (tel′ing), ''a.'' Effective; impressive; striking: as, a ''telling'' speech on tariff reform.

{{smaller block|Not Latimer, not Luther, struck more ''telling'' blows against false theology than did this brave singer.

In ''road-making'', to construct according to the method of road-making invented by Thomas Telford. See ''Telford pavement''. ¶ '''Telford pavement.''' A roadway devised by the Scotch engineer Thomas Telford (1757–1834). {{smaller block|The bottoming of the road consists of any durable stone, from 4 to 7 inches in dimensions, hand-laid upon the road-foundation. Between such stones smaller pieces are packed to complete a compact layer 7 inches deep in the middle of the road, and graduated to 4 inches in depth at the sides, to produce a uniform convexity. Upon this is spread, and rolled down, gravel composed of flints, the pieces being as nearly cubical in form as can be obtained, and none weighing more than six ounces. The rolling is continued till the surface is crushed and compacted to smoothness. The name is often contracted to ''telford''.}} ¶ '''telic''' (tel′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. τελικός, final, < τέλος, end, completion.] Noting a final end or purpose. See ''ecbatic''. ¶ '''teliconograph''' (tel-ī-kon′ō-grȧf), ''n.'' [< Gr. τῆλε, afar, + εἰκών, an image, + γράφειν, write. Cf. ''iconograph''.] Same as ''teleiconograph''. ¶ '''Telifera''' (tē-lif′e-rä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < L. ''tela'', web, + ''ferre'' = E. ''bear''1.] Same as ''Epithelaria''. ¶ '''Telinga''' (te-ling′gä), ''n.'' 1. One of the people living in the eastern part of the Deccan. ''Yule and Burnell''.—2†. [''l. c.''] A sepoy.—'''Telinga potato.''' {{smaller|See ''potato''.}} ¶ '''tell'''1 (tel), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''told'' (formerly or dial. sometimes ''telled'', ''telt''), ppr. ''telling''. [< ME. ''tellen'' (pret. ''tolde'', ''talde'', pp. ''told'', ''itold'', ''talden'', ''ytold''), < AS. ''tellan'' (pret. ''tealde'', pp. ''geteald'') = OS. ''tellian'' = OFries. ''tella'' = MD. D. ''tellen'', count, reckon, consider, = MLG. ''tellen'' = OHG. ''zellan'', MHG. ''zeln'', G. ''zählen'', number (''erzählen'', narrate), = Icel. ''telja'' = Sw. ''tälja'' = Dan. ''tælle'', number, tell; cf. Goth. ''talzjan'', instruct, direct; from the noun represented by ''tale''1: see ''tale''1, ''n.'' Cf. ''tale''1, ''v.'' For the forms ''tell'', ''told'', cf. ''sell'', ''sold''.] I. ''trans.'' 1. To number; count; enumerate; reckon one by one, or one after another: as, to ''tell'' a hundred; to ''tell'' one's beads. {{smaller block|Certeyn I hem never ''tolde''; For as fele eyen hadde she As fetheres upon foules be. {{right|''Chaucer'', House of Fame, l. 1380.}}}} {{smaller block|His custom was to ''tell'' over his herd of sea-calves at noon, and then to sleep. ''Bacon'', Physical Fables, vii.}} {{smaller block|He cannot be so innocent a coxcomb; He can ''tell'' ten, sure. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Nobody comes to visit him, he receives no letters, and ''tells'' his money morning and evening. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 264.}}}} 2. To recount; rehearse; narrate; relate: as, to ''tell'' a story. {{smaller block|Witnesse, ye Heavens, the truth of all that I have ''teld''! {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VII. vi. 27.}}}} {{smaller block|Life . . . is a tale ''Told'' by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 5. 27.}} {{smaller block|Masters, I have to ''tell'' a tale of woe, A tale of folly and of wasted life. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 5.}}}} 3. To make known; divulge; disclose; reveal; communicate: as, to ''tell'' a secret; to ''tell'' one's errand. {{smaller block|Now wul y ''telle'' the rygt Way to Jerusalem. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 125.}}}} {{smaller block|''Tell'' it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon. {{right|2 Sam. i. 20.}}}} {{smaller block|She never ''told'' her love, But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, Feed on her damask cheek. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., ii. 4. 113.}}}} {{smaller block|I wonder wha 's ''tauld'' that gay ladie The fashion into our countrie. {{right|''Lord Dingwall'' (Child's Ballads, I. 290).}}}} 4. To declare; say. {{smaller block|Who-so contrarieth treuthe he ''telleth'' in the gospel That God knoweth hym nouȝte, ne no seynte of heuene. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 55.}}}} 5. To put or express in words; recite; explain; make clear or plain. {{smaller block|And dede men for that deon [din] comen oute of deope graues, And ''tolden'' why that tempest so longe tyme durede. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 66.}}}} {{smaller block|I know, quoth he, what it meaneth, but I cannot ''tell'' it; I cannot express it. {{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.}}}} {{smaller block|Whoso ask'd her for his wife, His riddle ''told'' not, lost his life. {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, i., Prol., l. 38.}}}} {{smaller block|Few can ''tell'' his pedigree, Nor his subtill nature coster. {{right|''Marston and Barksted'', Insatiate Countess, v.}}}} 6. To discern so as to be able to say; distinguish; recognize; decide; determine: as, to ''tell'' one from another; she cannot ''tell'' which she likes best. {{smaller block|I could always ''tell'' if visitors had called in my absence. {{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 141.}}}} 7. To inform. {{smaller block|He seith that ye be sone aperceyvaunte of hym, and that ye sholde ''telle'' me what he is. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 74.}}}} {{smaller block|''Tell'' me, good Hobbinoll, what garres thee greete? {{right|''Spenser'', Shep. Cal., April.}}}} {{smaller block|I'll ''tell'' you as we pass along, That you will wonder what hath fortuned. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., v. 4. 168.}}}} 8. To give an order, command, or direction to; order; bid: as, I ''told'' him to stay at home. {{smaller block|Call for your casting-bottle, and place your mirror in your hat, as I ''told'' you. ''B. Jonson'', Cynthia's Revels, ii. 1.}} {{smaller block|It may be accepted as necessary for the comfort of all coachmen that a team should never start until ''told''. {{right|''New York Tribune'', May 11, 1890.}}}} 9. To assure; assert positively to. {{smaller block|They are burs, I can ''tell'' you. ''Shak.'', T. and C., iii. 2. 120.}} {{smaller block|Pshaw! I ''tell'' you 'tis no such thing—you are the man she wants, and nobody but you. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Duenna, ii. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|Let me ''tell'' you, you may drink worse French wine in many taverns in London than they have sometimes at this house. ''Cotton'', in Walton's Angler, ii. 227.}} 10†. To make account of: in phrases such as ''to tell no tale, to tell no dainty, to tell no store.'' {{smaller block|Vesselle of Sylver is there non: for thei ''telle'' no prys there of, to make no Vesselle offe. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 220.}}}} {{smaller block|I ne ''tolde no deyntee'' of hir love. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath's Tale, l. 208.}}}} '''Tell that to the marines.''' See ''marine''.—'''To tell noses.''' See ''nose''1.—'''To tell no store of†.''' See ''store''3.—'''To tell off,''' to count off; especially, to count off and detach, as for some special duty: as, a squad was ''told off'' to clear the streets.—'''To tell one's beads.''' See ''to bid beads'', under ''bead.''—'''To tell one's fortune,''' or '''to tell fortunes.''' See ''fortune.''—'''To tell one's own tale''' or '''story, to tell tale†, to tell tales out of school.''' See ''tale''1. '''=Syn.''' 3. {{smaller|To impart, report, repeat, mention, recite, publish.—4. ''Speak, State'', etc. See ''say''1.—7. To acquaint (with), apprise (of).}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' 1. To give an account; make report; speak; explain: with ''of.'' {{smaller block|Bothe of yonge and olde
Ful wel byloved, and wel folk ''of'' hire ''tolde.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 131.}}}} {{smaller block|That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and ''tell of'' all thy wondrous works. {{right|Ps. xxvi. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|This ancient and isolated city [Ragusa] has yet something more to ''tell of.'' {{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 240.}}}} {{smaller block|''Of'' the fruitful year
They ''told,'' and its delights. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 392.}}}} 2. To say; declare. {{smaller block|For hit aren murye-mouthede men mynstrales of heuene,
And godes boyes, bordiours as the bok ''telleth.'' {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), x. 127.}}}} 3. To talk; chat; gossip. [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|While I've been ''telling'' with you, here 've this little maid been and ate up all my sugar! {{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, xxx.}}}} 4. To tell tales; play the informer; inform; blab: with ''of'' or ''on'' before the person: as, if you do, I'll ''tell.'' [Now colloq.] {{smaller block|And David saved neither man nor woman alive, to bring tidings to Gath, saying, Lest they should ''tell on'' us, saying, So did David. {{right|1 Sam. xxvii. 11.}}}} {{smaller block|He didn't want to ''tell on'' Maggie, though he was angry with her; for Tom Tulliver was a lad of honor. {{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 5.}}}} 5. To act effectively; produce a marked effect or impression; count for something. {{smaller block|It's true, every year will ''tell'' upon him. He is over five-and-forty, you know.|{{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|It would seem that even pedantry and antiquarianism are welcomed when they ''tell'' on behalf of the other side.|{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 42.}}}} {{smaller block|Everybody knows that speeches are little, that debates are often nothing, in Congress and elsewhere; but votes ''tell''. It is the vote that men want.|{{right|''Bibliotheca Sacra'', XLVII. 544.}}}} '''To hear tell of.''' {{smaller|See ''hear''.}} '''tell'''1 (tel), ''n.'' [< ''tell''1, ''v.''] That which is told; account; narration; story; tale. [Rare.] {{smaller block|There, I am at the end of my ''tell!'' If I write on, it must be to ask questions.|{{right|''Walpole'', To Mann, April 4, 1743.}}}} {{smaller block|Little Barb'ry 's the very flower of the flock, accordin' to my ''tell''.|{{right|''E. Eggleston'', The Century, XXXV. 44.}}}} '''tell'''2 (tel), ''n.'' [< Ar. ''tell'', a hill.] A hill or mound: common in Oriental place-names. {{smaller block|The east bank of the Tigris, where gigantic ''tells'' or artificial mounds, and the traces of an ancient city wall, bore evident witness of fallen greatness.|{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVII. 511.}}}} '''tellable''' (tel′a-bl), ''a.'' [< ''tell''1 + ''-able.''] Capable of being told; worth telling. '''tell-bill-willy''' (tel′bil-wil″i), ''n.'' [Imitative.] The willet, ''Symphemia semipalmata.'' See cuts under ''willet'' and ''semipalmate.'' [Bahamas.] '''tell-clock†''' (tel′klok), ''n.'' [< ''tell''1, ''v.'', + obj. ''clock''2.] One who sits and counts the hours; an idler. {{smaller block|Is there no mean between busybodies and ''tell-clocks'', between factotums and faineants? {{right|''Rev. S. Ward'', Sermons, p. 131.}}}} ¶ '''telled''' (teld). An obsolete or provincial preterit of ''tell''1. ¶ '''tellen''' (tel′en), ''n.'' [< Sp. ''telina'' = F. ''telline'', < NL. ''Tellina'', < Gr. τελλίνη, a kind of shell-fish: see ''Tellina''.] A bivalve of the genus ''Tellina'' or of some of the related ''Tellinidæ''. ''P. P. Carpenter.'' ¶ '''teller''' (tel′ėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''tellere''; < ''tell''1 + ''-er''1.] 1. One who counts or enumerates. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') One of two or more persons, members of a deliberative or legislative body, appointed, when a division takes place, to count the votes cast for and against a particular proposal or measure. In the British House of Commons there are two tellers appointed for each party, of whom one for the ayes and another for the noes are associated to check each other in the telling. In the United States House of Representatives but one is appointed for each party. (''b'') One of four officers (styled ''talliers'' in old records) formerly employed in the British Exchequer to receive money payable to the king and to pay money payable by the king. The office was abolished in 1834 by 4 and 5 Will. IV., c. 15, and the duties of the four tellers are now performed by a controller-general of the receipt and issue of the Exchequer. See ''tallier''.}} {{smaller block|Sir Edward [Carey] was a gentleman of the Chamber, and one of the four ''Tellers'' of the Exchequer. {{right|''H. Hall'', Society in Elizabethan Age, ix.}}}} {{smaller block|(''c'') A functionary in a banking establishment whose business it is to receive or to pay money over the counter: as, a receiving ''teller''; a paying ''teller''.}} 2. One who tells, recounts, narrates, relates, or communicates something to others: as, a story-''teller''. {{smaller block|Sr Kenelm was a ''teller'' of strange things. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, June 18, 1670.}}}} {{smaller block|It is as Zara that the city is famous, because it is as Zara that its name appears in the pages of the great English ''teller'' of the tale.{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 121.}}}} '''tellership''' (tel′ėr-ship), ''n.'' [< ''teller'' + ''-ship''.] The office or post of teller; a position as teller. '''tellevas†''', ''n.'' See ''talevas''. '''Tellicherry bark.''' See ''conessi bark'', under ''bark''2. '''Tellina''' (te-lī′nä), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1758), < Gr. τελλίνη, a kind of shell-fish.] In ''conch.'', a genus of bivalve mollusks, typical of the family ''Tellinidæ''. {{smaller|The shell has a strong external ligament; it is generally thin and handsomely colored. The animal has very long siphons. There}} are many species, both living and extinct, of all coasts. See also cut under ''Tellinidæ''. [[File:century v08 p0023 c3f1.png|center|173px]] {{c|''Tellina lingua-felis'' (right valve).}} '''telling''' (tel′ing), ''a.'' Effective; impressive; striking: as, a ''telling'' speech on tariff reform. {{smaller block|Not Latimer, not Luther, struck more ''telling'' blows against false theology than did this brave singer. {{right|''Emerson'', Robert Burns.}}}} '''telling-house''' (tel′ing-hous), ''n.'' One of the rude cots in which shepherds on the moor meet at the end of the pasturing season, to tell or count their sheep. ''R. D. Blackmore'', Lorna Doone, ii., note. [Prov. Eng.] '''tellingly''' (tel′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a telling manner; so as to be effective; effectively. {{smaller block|The doctrine that poetry, not philosophy, is the true interpretation of life, is put ''tellingly'' and persuasively. {{right|''The Academy'', Dec. 1, 1888, p. 345.}}}} '''Tellinidæ''' (te-lin′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Tellina'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of bivalve mollusks, of which the genus ''Tellina'' is the type. {{smaller|The animal has the mantle-lobes wide open in front, but continued into very long, separate siphons behind; the labial palpi are large and triangular; the gills are united behind and appendiculate; the foot is tongue-shaped and compressed. The shell is nearly equivalve, and generally has cardinal and anterior and posterior lateral teeth.}} [[File:century v08 p0023 c3f2.png|center|142px]] {{c|''Tellina radiata.''}} ¶ '''tellinite''' (tel′i-nīt), ''n.'' [< ''Tellina'' + ''-ite''2.] A fossil shell of the genus ''Tellina'', or some similar one; a petrified tellen. '''telltale''' (tel′tāl), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''tell''1, ''v.'', + obj. ''tale''1.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One who officiously or heedlessly communicates information concerning the private affairs of others; one who tells that which is supposed to be secret or private; a blabber; an informer; a tale-bearer. {{smaller block|One that quarrells with no man, but for not pledging him, but takes all absurdities, and commits as many, and is no ''tell-tale'' next morning though hee remember it. {{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, An Ordinairie Honest [Fellow.}}}} {{smaller block|If you see your master wronged by any of your fellow-servants, be sure to conceal it, for fear of being called a ''tell-tale.'' ''Swift'', Advice to Servants (General Directions).}}
